claim: Approximately 2 billion people have been infected with human hepatitis B virus (HBV) worldwide.
source: Approximately 2 billion people have been infected with human hepatitis B virus (HBV) worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement about global HBV infection prevalence, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Over 350 million people currently are chronically infected with HBV and are at high risk for progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, or cancer.
source: Over 350 million people currently are chronically infected and are at high risk for progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, or cancer.
evidence: This is a statement about chronic HBV infection prevalence and associated risks, presented as established knowledge.

claim: More than 50% of liver cancers worldwide are attributed to HBV infection.
source: More than 50% of liver cancers worldwide are attributed to HBV infection.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of HBV to liver cancer, presented as established knowledge.

claim: HBV-related liver diseases cause approximately 1 million deaths per year.
source: HBV-related liver diseases remain a major public health problem, causing approximately 1 million deaths per year.
evidence: This is a statement about mortality from HBV-related diseases, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Individuals coinfected with HBV and HDV are at greater risk for rapid progression and severe disease.
source: Individuals coinfected with HBV and HDV are at greater risk for rapid progression and severe disease (Lavanchy, 2004; Hughes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lavanchy, 2004 and Hughes et al., 2011.

claim: HBV is an enveloped virus containing a small genome of 3.2 kb of partially double-stranded DNA encoding four overlapping reading frames.
source: HBV is an enveloped virus containing a small genome of 3.2 kb of partially double-stranded DNA encoding four overlapping reading frames.
evidence: This is a statement about HBV genome structure, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The HBV envelope consists of the small (S), middle (M), and large (L) envelope proteins, which are multiple transmembrane spanners sharing the same C-terminal domain corresponding to the S protein but differing at their N-terminal domains.
source: The HBV envelope consists of the small (S), middle (M), and large (L) envelope proteins, which are multiple transmembrane spanners sharing the same C-terminal domain corresponding to the S protein but differing at their N-terminal domains (Figure 1A) (Heermann et al., 1984; Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heermann et al., 1984 and Seeger et al., 2007, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: HDV is a small satellite RNA virus of HBV carrying all three HBV envelope proteins and can only propagate when coexisting with HBV.
source: HDV is a small satellite RNA virus of HBV carrying all three HBV envelope proteins and can only propagate when coexisting with HBV.
evidence: This is a statement about HDV biology, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The mechanism of viral entry of HDV is believed to be similar to that of HBV.
source: The mechanism of viral entry of HDV is believed to be similar to that of HBV, and HDV has been used as a surrogate for studying HBV infection at the entry level (Barrera et al., 2004; Sureau, 2006; Hughes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barrera et al., 2004; Sureau, 2006; and Hughes et al., 2011.

claim: The L protein and integrity of S protein are critical for HBV and HDV infections.
source: The L protein and integrity of S protein are critical for HBV and HDV infections.
evidence: This is a statement about viral protein requirements for infection, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The pre-S1 domain of the L protein is a key determinant for entry of both HBV and HDV and is believed to mediate viral interaction with the cellular receptor(s) on hepatocytes.
source: The pre-S1 domain of the L protein is a key determinant for entry of both HBV and HDV and is believed to mediate viral interaction with the cellular receptor(s) on hepatocytes (Gripon et al., 1995; Le Seyec et al., 1999; Chouteau et al., 2001; Blanchet and Sureau, 2007; Le Duff et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A number of HBV receptor candidates have been reported in the past, but none has been confirmed to be functional in supporting viral infection.
source: Although a number of HBV receptor candidates have been reported in the past, none has been confirmed to be functional in supporting viral infection (Glebe and Urban, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glebe and Urban, 2007.

claim: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) in the pre-S1 domain did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes (PTHs).
source: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes (PTHs) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids.
source: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1C.

claim: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs.
source: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs.
source: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Western blotting using 2D3 as a probe revealed several bands including a major smeared band with apparent molecular weight of ∼65 kDa in the WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked sample.
source: Western blotting using 2D3 as a probe revealed several bands including a major smeared band with apparent molecular weight of ∼65 kDa in the WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked sample.
evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from Western blotting.

claim: The 65-kDa band shifted to ∼43 kDa upon treatment with the deglycosylation enzyme PNGase F.
source: The 65-kDa band shifted to ∼43 kDa upon treatment with the deglycosylation enzyme PNGase F (Figure 2A, left), indicating that it is highly N-glycosylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The WTb cross-linked protein apparently contained no intermolecular disulfide bonds as it migrated similarly under both nonreducing and reducing conditions.
source: The WTb cross-linked protein apparently contained no intermolecular disulfide bonds as it migrated similarly under both nonreducing and reducing conditions (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide but not its N9K mutant peptide effectively competed with WTb for cross-linking to the 65-kDa band.
source: The non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide but not its N9K mutant peptide effectively competed with WTb for cross-linking to the 65-kDa band (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cross-linked protein from PTHs decreased in abundance rapidly over time during culture.
source: The cross-linked protein from PTHs decreased in abundance rapidly over time during culture (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Bands with slightly smaller molecular weights than those seen in the PTH cells were also observed in PHHs.
source: Bands with slightly smaller molecular weights than those seen in the PTH cells were also observed in PHHs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two different tryptic peptide fragments, which were identified from both the ∼65-kDa and ∼43-kDa bands, matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
source: Two different tryptic peptide fragments, which were identified from both the ∼65-kDa and ∼43-kDa bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart and has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus.
source: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart and has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both human NTCP (hNTCP) and tsNTCP could be efficiently cross-linked by WTb but not N9Kb when expressed in 293T cells.
source: Both human NTCP (hNTCP) and tsNTCP could be efficiently cross-linked by WTb but not N9Kb when expressed in 293T cells as shown by Western blotting with the anti-WTb antibody 2D3 as well as an anti-C9 antibody recognizing the C-terminal C9 tag of the recombinant hNTCP and tsNTCP proteins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WTb but not the control N9Kb peptide bound to 293T cells expressing a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged tsNTCP (tsNTCP-EGFP) and co-localized with tsNTCP-EGFP on the cell surface.
source: WTb but not the control N9Kb peptide bound to 293T cells expressing a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged tsNTCP (tsNTCP-EGFP) and co-localized with tsNTCP-EGFP on the cell surface. This binding was readily competed off by the free Myr-47/WT peptide (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A native pre-S1 peptide specifically recognized the human hepatocellular carcinoma Huh-7 cell line transfected with hNTCP.
source: Moreover, a native pre-S1 peptide specifically recognized the human hepatocellular carcinoma Huh-7 cell line transfected with hNTCP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Huh-7 cells transfected with either tsNTCP or hNTCPs had markedly increased HDV binding to the cells.
source: Consistently, Huh-7 cells transfected with either tsNTCP or hNTCPs had markedly increased HDV binding to the cells.
evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from HDV binding assays.

claim: The Myr-47/WT peptide readily competed with binding of the wild-type HDV, whereas a noninfectious mutant HDV virus bearing a single N9K mutation in the pre-S1 domain of its L envelope protein failed to bind either hNTCP- or tsNTCP-expressing Huh-7 cells.
source: The Myr-47/WT peptide readily competed with binding of the wild-type HDV, whereas a noninfectious mutant HDV virus bearing a single N9K mutation in the pre-S1 domain of its L envelope protein failed to bind either hNTCP- or tsNTCP-expressing Huh-7 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When tsNTCP mRNA level was reduced to ∼30% in tsNTCP siRNA-transfected cells, total HDV RNA copies were markedly reduced in these cells comparing to those transfected with control siRNA.
source: When tsNTCP mRNA level was reduced to ∼30% in tsNTCP siRNA-transfected cells (Figure 4A, upper-left), total HDV RNA copies were markedly reduced in these cells comparing to those transfected with control siRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA copies were greatly reduced in cells transfected with tsNTCP-specific siRNA but not the control siRNA.
source: As shown in Figure 4A (upper-middle panel), both HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA copies were greatly reduced in cells transfected with tsNTCP-specific siRNA but not the control siRNA, indicating that tsNTCP is required for de novo HDV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lenti-VSV-G virus infection, for which viral entry is mediated by glycoprotein protein G of VSV, was not affected in the tsNTCP- and siRNA-transfected cells.
source: By contrast, lenti-VSV-G virus infection, for which viral entry is mediated by glycoprotein protein G of VSV, was not affected in the tsNTCP- and siRNA-transfected cells (Figure 4A, upper-right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both HBsAg and HBeAg levels were markedly reduced by transfection of tsNTCP-specific but not a control siRNA at all three time points tested.
source: As shown in Figure 4A (lower-left), both HBsAg and HBeAg levels were markedly reduced by transfection of tsNTCP-specific but not a control siRNA at all three time points tested, demonstrating that tsNTCP expression is required for bona fide HBV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs.
source: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs, as shown by the kinetics of HBeAg (Figure 4A, lower-right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction.
source: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction (Figure 4B, upper-left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs.
source: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs (Figure 4B, upper-right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HBV infection was inhibited by hNTCP knockdown in HepaRG cells as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points, as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA quantified at the end of the experiment.
source: Similarly, HBV infection was also inhibited as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points (Figure 4B, lower-left), as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA (Figure 4B, lower-right) quantified at the end of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection in PHHs, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency.
source: Consistently, knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency. Both viral antigens and viral RNAs were decreased in cells transfected with hNTCP-specific siRNAs but not with the control siRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
source: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
evidence: This is a statement about NTCP expression in cell lines, presented as an observation.

claim: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes.
source: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human NTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells supported HDV infection with an efficiency comparable to that of PTHs; nearly 10% of cells were infected as shown by staining of the HDV delta antigen that mainly locates in cell nuclei, whereas Huh-7 cells transfected with a vector plasmid allowed no HDV infection.
source: Human NTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells supported HDV infection with an efficiency comparable to that of PTHs; nearly 10% of cells were infected as shown by staining of the HDV delta antigen that mainly locates in cell nuclei, whereas Huh-7 cells transfected with a vector plasmid allowed no HDV infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The infection of HDV in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells could be blocked by known HBV entry inhibitors, such as pre-S1 lipopeptide and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG).
source: Moreover, the infection could be blocked by known HBV entry inhibitors, such as pre-S1 lipopeptide and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), demonstrating a genuine infection of HDV mediated by HBV envelope proteins on these cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HDV RNAs, including antigenomic RNA that is only produced during HDV replication, rapidly increased over time in the infected hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells.
source: HDV RNAs, including antigenomic RNA that is only produced during HDV replication, rapidly increased over time in the infected cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The infection efficiency of HDV in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells correlated with both the inoculation dose of HDV and the expression level of hNTCP.
source: Moreover, the infection efficiency correlated with both the inoculation dose of HDV (Figure 5E) and the expression level of hNTCP (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells.
source: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells. The entry inhibitor Myr-59 blocked the infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: About 5–10% of stable HepG2-hNTCP cells were infected with HBV as revealed by intracellular staining of HBsAg, whereas there was no HBV infection in the parental HepG2 cells.
source: More efficient HBV infection was achieved on stable HepG2-hNTCP cells with about 5–10% of the cells being infected as revealed by intracellular staining of HBsAg, whereas there was no HBV infection in the parental HepG2 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HBV entry inhibitors, in particular the Myr-59 peptide and 17B9, efficiently inhibited the infection of HepG2-hNTCP cells.
source: HBV entry inhibitors, in particular the Myr-59 peptide and 17B9, efficiently inhibited the infection (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The infection efficiency of HBV in HepG2-hNTCP cells as evidenced by HBV total and 3.5 kb RNA levels correlated with the inoculation dose.
source: The infection efficiency as evidenced by HBV total and 3.5 kb RNA levels correlated with the inoculation dose.
evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from HBV infection assays.

claim: The formation of HBV covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is a replicative intermediate and transcriptional template for production of viral RNAs, was confirmed by Southern blot analysis in HepG2-hNTCP cells.
source: Moreover, the formation of HBV covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is a replicative intermediate and transcriptional template for production of viral RNAs, was confirmed by Southern blot analysis (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HBV cccDNA became detectable at 24 hr post-infection in HepG2-hNTCP cells, markedly increased at day 3 post-infection and maintained a relatively stable level for the rest of the time points examined.
source: The cccDNA became detectable at 24 hr post-infection. It markedly increased at day 3 post-infection and maintained a relatively stable level for the rest of the time points examined, whereas the formation of HBV cccDNA was completely abolished if entry inhibitor Myr-59 was included with the initial virus inoculation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: HBV RNA levels of the 3.5 kb transcript and the total HBV transcripts in the infected HepG2-hNTCP cells gradually increased during first several days of infection and reached a steady level after day 5.
source: Consistently, HBV RNA levels of the 3.5 kb transcript and the total HBV transcripts in the infected HepG2-hNTCP cells gradually increased during first several days of infection and reached a steady level after day 5 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) NTCP (mkNTCP) shares high protein sequence identity with hNTCP (96.3%).
source: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) NTCP (mkNTCP) shares high protein sequence identity with hNTCP (96.3%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: mkNTCP neither supports HDV infection nor pre-S1 peptide (Myr-59) binding.
source: However, mkNTCP neither supports HDV infection nor pre-S1 peptide (Myr-59) binding (Figure 7A), consistent with the known narrow species specificity of the virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Alteration of five residues of hNTCP between aa 157–165 and its monkey counterpart (from KGIVISLVL to GRIILSLVP) completely abolished Myr-59 binding and the ability to support HDV infection.
source: Whereas most mutations did not significantly interfere with Myr-59 binding or HDV infection, alteration of five residues of hNTCP between aa 157–165 and its monkey counterpart (from KGIVISLVL to GRIILSLVP, distinct residues are underlined) completely abolished Myr-59 binding and the ability to support HDV infection.
evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Replacing the motif of aa 167–156 in mkNTCP with the corresponding human residues converted mkNTCP to an efficient receptor for HDV infection.
source: Remarkably, replacing the motif of aa 167–156 in mkNTCP with the corresponding human residues converted mkNTCP to an efficient receptor for HDV infection (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HBV infection was abolished on HepG2 cells expressing hNTCP carrying monkey-like mutations, GRIILSLVP, while mkNTCP-bearing human residues KGIVISLVL within the motif of aa 157–165 largely restored HBV infection.
source: Similar to HDV, HBV infection was also abolished on HepG2 cells expressing hNTCP carrying monkey-like mutations, GRIILSLVP, while mkNTCP-bearing human residues KGIVISLVL within the motif of aa 157–165 largely restored HBV infection (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Residues between 157 and 165 of NTCP are crucial for binding to the receptor-binding region of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein of HBV, and critically contribute to NTCP-mediated HBV and HDV infections.
source: These data show that residues between 157 and 165 of NTCP are crucial for binding to the receptor-binding region of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein of HBV, and critically contribute to NTCP-mediated HBV and HDV infections.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the mutagenesis experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: NTCP is a functional receptor for both HBV and HDV.
source: Our results demonstrate that NTCP is a functional receptor for HBV and HDV.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes through engaging an unknown cellular component, most likely a viral receptor.
source: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes through engaging an unknown cellular component, most likely a viral receptor (Barrera et al., 2005; Glebe et al., 2005; Gripon et al., 2005; Engelke et al., 2006; Schulze et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
source: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about NTCP classification, presented as established knowledge.

claim: NTCP is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.
source: It is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids (Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994; Stieger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994 and Stieger, 2011.

claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops.
source: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops (Mareninova et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mareninova et al., 2005 and Hu et al., 2011.

claim: NTCP is mainly expressed in the liver.
source: It is mainly expressed in the liver (Stieger, 2011), consistent with the liver tropism of HBV and HDV.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stieger, 2011.

claim: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
source: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes (Stieger et al., 1994), a location that fits well with its receptor role for blood-borne HBV and HDV.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stieger et al., 1994.

claim: HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate.
source: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008), our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific, and NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schulze et al., 2007 and Leistner et al., 2008.

claim: NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
source: Consistent with previous reports on primary cultures of rat hepatocytes (Liang et al., 1993; Rippin et al., 2001), NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 1993 and Rippin et al., 2001, and by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues.
source: This may at least partially explain the observations that primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues (Gripon et al., 1988; Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gripon et al., 1988 and Seeger et al., 2007.

claim: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005) and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997 and Zollner et al., 2005.

claim: NTCP expression is inversely correlated with the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis.
source: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005) and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee and Kim, 2007.

claim: About 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected with HBV at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs.
source: As shown by intracellular staining of HBV core antigen (HBcAg) on day 8 post-infection, about 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors, whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable.
source: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors, whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums, and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection.
source: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums, and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; and Boehm et al., 2005.

claim: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period in HepG2-NTCP cells.
source: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period.
evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from viral DNA quantification assays.

claim: Only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs.
source: Similarly, only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection with culture medium collected from infected HepG2-NTCP cells.
source: In line with the low HBV viral DNA level in the medium inoculum, very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), indicating that only very limited HBV infection might have occurred, which may be attributed to the low multiplicity of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri) are the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees.
source: Primary hepatocytes isolated from treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri), the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees (Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; Glebe et al., 2003), were used as target cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; and Glebe et al., 2003.

claim: HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells.
source: Human hepatoma cell line HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gripon et al., 2002.

claim: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks.
source: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gripon et al., 2002.

claim: HDV is enveloped by HBV envelope proteins and can only infect target cells in a single round in the absence of HBV.
